screened.idea: Add an NPU/FPGA co-processor for prefill GEMMs and overlap per-layer GEMM compute with O_DIRECT prefetch of the next layer's coalesced expert blobs, so time-to-first-token (TTFT) falls from compute-bound (about 109 s) to I/O-bound (about 29 s). It is prefill-only. Decode stays at about 2-4 tok/s, and the extra hardware is a purchase, not an offline model change.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 3.7x on TTFT (109 s to 29 s) for a 500-token prompt. Claims of 1.65x to 9x across 21 runs. No decode tok/s gain.
screened.arithmetic: Recomputed from our data with python3. The 109 s uses 6e12 / 55e9 = 109 s. But 55 GFLOP/s is the decode rate, a batch-1 GEMV that is memory-bound. Our measured batched prefill is 311 GFLOP/s on OLMoE, so 6e12 / 311e9 = 19.3 s. I/O is 69 GB / 2.4 GB/s = 28.8 s, or 22.3 s at 3.1 GB/s, or about 44 s at the 1.56 GB/s that 1 MiB reads give (an expert is stored as 3 tensors of about 0.9 MB). Prefill with 500 tokens touches nearly every expert once, so about 50-69 GB must be read. Result: with batched prefill and overlap, TTFT is about max(19 s, 22-44 s), which is already I/O-bound on the CPU alone. Adding an NPU only removes a compute term that is already hidden. The real gain from the NPU is about 1.0x on TTFT (at most 1.0-1.5x if the overlap is imperfect). The 109 s baseline is fictional. The 3.7x comes from a wrong baseline. The proposal's 900 GFLOP/s only lowers the compute term from 19 s to 6.7 s, which sits under the 22-44 s I/O floor.
screened.arithmetic_error: Wrong baseline: it uses the decode-GEMV rate of 55 GFLOP/s for prefill, which is batched and runs at 311 GFLOP/s, 5.7x higher. Wrong metric: the gain is TTFT, not tok/s, and decode is unchanged. Ignored bound: the I/O floor of 22-44 s remains. It also uses the 4 MiB read rate (2.4 GB/s) for files whose tensors are about 0.9 MB. The FPGA/NPU hardware purchase also breaks the offline-model-change lever. This duplicates the first screen's finding on layer-major or expert-major prefill, where compute of 19 s at 311 GFLOP/s is overlapped under the read and the bound is the disk (idea_screen_raw.json).

real_multiplier.gb8_laptop: TTFT about 1.0x vs our best path (layer-major prefill with explicit reads), because it is already I/O-bound at 22-44 s. Decode tok/s 1.0x.
real_multiplier.gb16_laptop: Same: TTFT about 1.0x, decode 1.0x. RAM barely changes the full 50-69 GB prefill read.
real_multiplier.gb32_desktop: Same: TTFT about 1.0x, decode 1.0x. 69 GB still does not fit in RAM.
real_multiplier.bound: Disk read rate over 50-69 GB (22-44 s). Decode is bound at 4.6 tok/s by compute and 1.30 GB/token by reads, and an NPU does not change that.
real_multiplier.vs: our best path (explicit large reads + LRU + overlapped batched prefill). Versus plain mmap, TTFT gain comes from read size and layer-major order, not from the NPU.

screened.idea: Put int4/int8 expert GEMV engines in computational-storage FPGA drives (two U.2 SmartSSD-class devices, ~34 GB of experts each) so expert weights are read from NAND inside the drive and only about 4 KB activations and partial sums cross PCIe. This removes the host-side I/O term (1.3 GB per token at 2.4 GB/s is 0.54 s) and leaves compute only, the 4.57 tok/s ceiling, claimed as a 2.5-3x gain (list of run claims runs from 1.6 to 20).
screened.claimed_multiplier: 2.5-3x (1.8 to 4.6 tok/s) at 8 GB RAM; run claims range 1.6-20x
screened.arithmetic: I did not run code. I recomputed from the corrected facts. (1) The 1.8 tok/s baseline (1.3 GB / 2.4 GB/s = 0.54 s) is the serial no-overlap figure. Our best path at 8 GB (explicit 4 MiB reads + LRU) is already 2.18 tok/s serial and 4.16 tok/s overlapped. So the gain over our best path is 4.57/2.18 = 2.1x serial and 4.57/4.16 = 1.1x overlapped, not 2.5-3x. (2) The weights do not vanish. They must still be read from NAND inside the drive. 1.3 GB per token split over 2 drives is 0.65 GB per drive. At about 3 GB/s internal flash bandwidth per drive (we measured 3.1 GB/s host reads on the Mac NVMe; SmartSSD-class drives are PCIe x4 devices with the same NAND), that is 0.22 s per token, the same as the compute time (0.22 s). So the in-drive bound is about 1/0.22 = 4.6 tok/s only if both drives are perfectly balanced and the FPGA keeps up. Expert load per drive is uneven, because 10 of 512 experts are chosen, so some layers hit one drive harder. Realistic is 3-4 tok/s. (3) Two ordinary NVMe drives striped (RAID0) give 2 x 3.1 = 6.2 GB/s host-side. That is 1.3 / 6.2 = 0.21 s of I/O, the same 4.6 tok/s ceiling, with no FPGA. The FPGA adds nothing over striping, because the flash bandwidth is the same and the PCIe link is not the limit. (4) 55 GFLOP/s is the measured CPU rate. Moving the expert part does not make it additive. Dense layers (~1.9 GB resident, roughly 7 of 12 GFLOP) stay on the CPU. FPGA expert compute is about 5 GFLOP per token (my split estimate), well under what an FPGA can do, but the dispatch overhead for 480 slice calls per token is unmeasured (0.22 s / 480 = 0.46 ms per slice including a round trip). (5) The claim of 'removes the 8 GB RAM bound' is true, but the same applies to any RAM size. RAM no longer matters, which also means no benefit from more RAM.
screened.arithmetic_error: Wrong baseline: the 1.8 tok/s starting point is a serial, no-overlap figure at a 2.4 GB/s read rate, but our best path overlaps I/O and compute and already reaches 4.16 tok/s overlapped at 8 GB (2.18 serial). Ignored bound: the flash read rate inside the drive. 0.65 GB per drive per token at about 3 GB/s is 0.22 s, equal to the compute floor, so the idea hits the same ceiling as plain striping, not a new one. Also mixes the CPU's 55 GFLOP/s with FPGA compute (the answer admits this is unproven), and ignores per-slice dispatch cost across 480 slices per token.

Step 1 (free, arithmetic): confirm the striping equivalence with a Python recompute using the corrected numbers: python3 -I -c "io=1.3; print('1 NVMe',1/(io/3.1),'2 NVMe',1/(io/6.2),'ceiling',55/12)". Step 2 (cheap, local): check that the Mac NVMe read rate saturates with parallel reads of 2.7 MB extents on the Qwen3-30B file, e.g. a python script in /tmp/screen2-new-1/ that opens ~/Downloads/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Q4_K_M.gguf, issues os.pread of 2.7 MB at random aligned offsets with F_NOCACHE set via fcntl, using 1, 4, 8 and 16 threads, and prints GB/s. screened.idea: Quantise expert weights with 8-dim vector quantisation (2 bit per 8 weights from a 256-entry codebook, about 2.4 bpw with scales). Reuse the codes as lookup-table indices. Per 8-wide activation chunk, precompute the dot of the chunk with all 256 codewords, then each weight block costs one table gather plus one add instead of 8 FMAs. Claimed: bytes 4.3 to 2.4 bpw and ops about 8x fewer (12 to 1.5 GFLOP/token), so the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling is lifted. The family's own gaps flag the 55 GFLOP/s-equivalent gather kernel as unproven.
screened.claimed_multiplier: Claims in the family range 1.3x to 9x. The headline is about 8x fewer ops and about 3x fewer bytes, implying about 8x compute ceiling (37 tok/s asserted).
screened.arithmetic: Bytes: 4.3/2.4 = 1.79x, not about 3x (1.3 GB to 0.73 GB is 1.78x). Ops: the accumulate count per weight block is unchanged, so only the multiply goes away. The 8x is 8 MACs replaced by 1 gather+add, but the baseline is not an FMA loop. llama.cpp decode uses int8 maddubs dot kernels doing about 32 weights per instruction group, roughly 20 weights/cycle/core. An AVX2 vpgatherdd does 8 lookups (64 weights) in roughly 5+ cycles, about 13 weights/cycle, and needs the table in L1 (256 entries x 2 B x 256 chunks = 128 KB per 2048-wide input, so it spills to L2). The table build costs 2048 MACs per 8-wide chunk, which amortises only with more than about 1000 output rows (experts here are about 768 wide). Realistic gather kernel speed is 0.7-1.5x of the current dot kernel, not 8x. Model with corrected facts (explicit 4 MiB reads at 2.38 GB/s, compute ceiling 4.57, 1.3 GB at 4.3 bpw): 8 GB baseline LRU 2.1 footprints, hit 0.56, disk 0.57 GB, 0.24 s, so serial 2.18 and overlap 4.16 tok/s. With 2.4 bpw only (LUT kernel 1x): footprint 0.73 GB, cache about 3.8 footprints, hit about 0.74, disk 0.19 GB, 0.08 s, so serial 1/(0.08+0.219) = 3.3 and overlap min(4.57, 12) = 4.57. That is 1.5x serial and 1.1x overlap, and it comes from bytes (the bpw lever already modelled), not from the LUT. If the gather kernel were 1.5x faster than the dot kernel the ceiling becomes 6.9 and overlap at 8 GB is about 6.9 = 1.65x of 4.16. At 16 and 32 GB the cache is 9-21 footprints, hit about 0.95-0.99, I/O is negligible and speed equals the compute ceiling, so the gain equals the kernel ratio only. (Mental calculation from the corrected facts, not re-run on the traces.)
screened.arithmetic_error: (1) Bytes cut claimed as about 3x but is 1.79x. (2) Op count cut counts only multiplies and ignores accumulation, the table build and the L1/L2 spill. (3) Baseline treated as an fp FMA loop at 55 GFLOP/s, but our 55 GFLOP/s is the measured quantised-dot rate, so 8x is against the wrong baseline. (4) Bytes and ops gains multiplied as if independent, but at 16 and 32 GB I/O is already hidden, so the bytes gain does nothing there. (5) The cache-hit gain from smaller experts is the bpw lever already in combo_model.py. (6) Quality loss of 2-bit VQ on a 125B MoE is not costed.

screened.idea: Persist the exact KV cache of a finished prompt to disk, keyed by a hash of the token prefix, model, quantization and router. On a repeated or shared-prefix prompt, load the KV from disk and skip prefill. Decode is untouched, so it only cuts time to first token (TTFT) on cache hits.
screened.claimed_multiplier: More than 3x TTFT on hits. The family's claims list runs 1.7x to 100x, which cannot be tied to this idea's own text. Decode tok/s is not changed (the idea says so itself).
screened.arithmetic:
Not run on the traces. The router traces are decode-only and say nothing about KV size or prefill, so I recomputed by hand from the facts in the task text and the Qwen3-30B-A3B shape (48 layers, 4 KV heads, head dim 128, fp16 KV, config recalled from memory and not checked on disk).
KV size: 2 x 48 x 4 x 128 x 2 B = 98 KB per token, so 500 tokens is about 49 MB. The 125B model's config is unknown; at 2-3x that per-token size it is about 100-150 MB. The family's '1-2 GB for 500 tokens' is therefore about 10-20x too high, and replay is then I/O-trivial: 49-150 MB at 3.1 GB/s is about 0.02-0.05 s.
Cold TTFT: the family says 40-110 s. Its compute floor of 109 s uses the 55 GFLOP/s decode rate, but batched prefill measured about 311 GFLOP/s on OLMoE. 6 TFLOP / 311 GFLOP/s is about 19 s of compute. The I/O floor is 69 GB / 3.1 GB/s (explicit reads) is about 22 s, or 29 s at the 2.4 GB/s the family used. So cold TTFT is about 25-35 s on the best path, not 40-110 s. The baseline is inflated by 1.5-4x.
Hit TTFT: load KV (0.05 s) plus one decode step (480 expert slices, 1.3 GB at 3.1 GB/s is about 0.42 s, or about 0.22 s compute at 4.6 tok/s if overlapped) is about 0.5-0.7 s. The family's 1-2 s is pessimistic on the hit side too.
Real ratio on a hit: about 30 s / 0.6 s = 40-50x on the best path, or about 60 s+ on plain mmap. The 3x claim understates a hit and overstates the baseline. The honest statement is 'huge on exact hits, 1.0x otherwise'.
Effect on tok/s: zero. Over a 200-token answer at about 2-4 tok/s (50-100 s), a 30 s prefill saving is a 1.3-1.6x cut in total request wall time, and only on a hit.
screened.arithmetic_error: Three errors. (1) Wrong baseline: the cold compute floor uses the 55 GFLOP/s decode rate instead of the measured batched-prefill rate of about 311 GFLOP/s, which inflates the 109 s figure about 5.7x. (2) KV size is asserted at 1-2 GB with no derivation; GQA gives about 50-150 MB. (3) The headline is conditional on a hit, with no hit rate given. screened.idea: Hide expert I/O under compute by predicting layer l+1's experts from layer l's chosen experts (claimed precision 0.55), prefetching ~0.72 GB during the 0.22 s compute window, then reading only about 0.58 GB of misses. screened.claimed_multiplier: 2.3x (4.1 vs ~1.8 tok/s); claims in the family run 1.5x to 8x
screened.arithmetic:
The idea's own gaps hold. 0.72 GB at 2.4 GB/s is 0.30 s, longer than the 0.22 s compute window, so it cannot be fully hidden. Wrong predictions (45% of the prefetch) use the same disk bandwidth. Total bytes = 0.72 prefetched + 0.58 missed = 1.30 GB, so nothing is saved; it is still disk-bound at 0.54 s.

Two further problems:
(1) The lead time is one layer, not one token. Layer l+1's prediction needs layer l's router output, so the window is about 4.6 ms (0.2186 s / 48 layers) against 27 MB per layer (8.7 ms at 3.1 GB/s).
(2) The 0.55 is not held out. I rebuilt a layer-to-layer co-occurrence predictor (prefetch top-8 experts at layer l+1 given the 8 chosen at layer l) on the three Qwen3-30B traces:
- In-sample precision is 0.57-0.59, which matches the 0.55.
- Trained on the other two prompts and tested on the third, precision is 0.43 (db), 0.31 (story) and 0.37 (code).
- Predicting only 4 experts gives precision 0.18-0.26.
- Previous-token persistence is 0.42-0.46.
- This is the 128-expert model; the 512-expert target will probably be lower.

I ran an event simulation at /tmp/screen2-new-4/s.py. It uses per-layer LRU, a shared FIFO disk at 3.1 GB/s, 3.39 MB per slice (1.3 GB per token), 4.57 tok/s compute split over 48 layers, prefetch issued when layer l's data is ready, and a held-out predictor. Results (db/story/code), tok/s without prefetch vs with prefetch m=4 vs with prefetch m=8:
- 2.1 footprints: no prefetch 2.47/2.58/2.43; m=4 2.65/2.69/2.57 (x1.07/1.04/1.06); m=8 2.50/2.38/2.39 (x1.02/0.92/0.98). Bytes per token rise from 0.58 to 0.76-1.04 GB.
- 4 footprints: no prefetch 3.32/3.53/3.10; with prefetch x1.00-1.02.
- 7.5 footprints: x1.00 (4.3 tok/s, at the compute ceiling).
The idea is the "overlap" lever already in combo_model.py (phi, 0.55 precision). That model uses max(comp, pre) over a whole-token window, which gives a bigger gain than the one-layer window allows.

The prefetch lever is the same one the model covers: 4.16 vs 2.18 tok/s at 8 GB assumes perfect, unlimited-lead overlap.
screened.arithmetic_error:
1) Double count: the 0.72 GB of prefetch is counted as hidden, and the same bytes are then subtracted from the 1.3 GB total. The 0.55 precision means 45% of prefetched bytes are wasted disk time.
2) Ignored bound: the 0.30 s prefetch is longer than the 0.22 s window, and disk bandwidth is the shared limit.
3) Wrong window: the lead time is one layer (about 4.6 ms), not a token.
4) Wrong baseline: 1.8 tok/s is uncached. The LRU already removes 44% of bytes at 2.1 footprints, 79% at 4.
5) The 0.55 is in-sample. Held-out it is 0.31-0.43.
6) The "42% same-token repeat" is the previous-token persistence, which the LRU already captures.

screened.idea: Per MoE layer, factor all 512 experts onto one shared low-rank basis W0 kept resident, and store each expert only as a 2-3 bit residual on disk. A token then streams about 0.36 GB instead of 1.3 GB (3.6x fewer bytes), which the idea says lifts the I/O-bound rate from about 1.85 to about 6.6 tok/s. It is a combined weight-compression plus fewer-FLOPs claim, and it is lossy.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 3.6x bytes, 3.5x tok/s (1.85 to 6.6 tok/s) at 8 GB
screened.arithmetic:
I did not run the trace tools. The decisive numbers are already in the facts, so this is closed-form arithmetic on them.

- Bytes: 480 slices x 2.7 MB = 1.30 GB per token. The slice size is about 4.3 bpw.
- A 2-3 bit residual alone is 2.5/4.3 = 0.58 of the bytes, which is 0.76 GB per token, or 1.7x fewer bytes, even if the shared basis costs nothing. The claimed 0.36 GB needs about 1.2 bpw of residual, which is not a 2-3 bit residual. That is an arithmetic inconsistency.
- Compute is untouched. Every residual still goes through full-size matmuls, plus the extra basis matmuls, so the ceiling stays at or below 4.57 tok/s (55 GFLOP/s over 12 GFLOP per token). The claimed 6.6 tok/s is above that bound, so it is impossible. The claim also uses an inconsistent baseline: 1.85 tok/s is its own I/O-only figure, not our best path.
- Recompute at 8 GB for our best path (explicit 4 MiB reads plus LRU at 2.1 footprints, hit 0.56). Disk bytes are 0.44 x 1.30 = 0.57 GB. At 2.38 GB/s that is 0.24 s of I/O plus 0.219 s of compute, so 2.18 tok/s serial (4.16 overlap).
- With 1.7x fewer bytes: I/O is 0.14 s, giving 1/(0.14+0.219) = 2.8 tok/s serial (1.28x). Overlap is min(4.57, 2.38/0.335 = 7.1) = 4.57, a 1.10x gain over 4.16.
- With the full 3.6x (not credible): I/O is 0.067 s, giving 3.5 tok/s serial (1.6x) and 4.57 overlap (1.10x).
- Caching still multiplies the savings. The two do not compound as 3.6 x 3.6.
screened.arithmetic_error:
Four errors:
1. A 3.6x byte cut is turned into a 3.6x tok/s gain while the compute ceiling of 4.57 tok/s is ignored (6.6 > 4.57).
2. The baseline is mixed: 1.85 tok/s is an I/O-only figure, not our best path of 2.18 serial / 4.16 overlap.
3. 2-3 bit residuals give at most 1.7x fewer bytes, not 3.6x.
4. The cache hit rate (0.56 at 2.1 footprints) is ignored. The comparison should be cache-adjusted bytes, not raw bytes.

I ran <tinyram-llm>/tools/combo_model.py (likely scenario) with its 'exit' lever set to 0.33. The lever scales expert bytes, dense FLOPs and expert FLOPs by the same factor, which is what this idea does. - 8 GB: 11.6 / 12.7 tok/s vs 2.49 best = 4.65x / 5.1x (vs mmap 0.53: 22x / 24x).

- 32 GB: 12.95 / 13.45 tok/s vs 4.27 = 3.0x / 3.15x (vs mmap 2.75: 4.7x / 4.9x).

screened.idea: During expert-major prefill, keep the streamed experts in a session-pinned RAM set (about 20 GB of a 24 GB budget). The claim is that decode then reads RAM instead of NVMe and runs at the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling, about 3x. This is the "95% prefill-touch set resident for decode" idea from the first screen, and PrefillHot in the SeqMoE paper (arXiv 2609.12978).
screened.claimed_multiplier: about 3x (range 1.5 to 512 in the family claims)
screened.arithmetic:
The 3x compares 4.6 tok/s with an assumed 2-4 tok/s baseline, which is really 1.2-2.3x. It also assumes zero decode I/O.
The gaps list says a 20 GB pin holds only 29% of the experts, so decode would mostly miss. That undersells it. I ran the first-W-token frequency top-N pin per layer on the 3 Qwen3-30B traces, scored on the next 20 tokens (script /tmp/screen2-new-7/a.py). The 128-expert traces are only a decode-only proxy for prefill.
- 29% pinned, W=64: 0.81 / 0.87 / 0.82 hit (db / story / code).
- 29% pinned, W=128: 0.86 / 0.85 / 0.84 hit.
- 15% pinned: 0.57-0.64.
- 50% pinned: 0.94-0.97.
So pinning does work, but it is the same lever as the LRU that is already in the best path. 29% of 128 is 37 slots per layer, about 4.6 footprints, and LRU at 4 footprints gives 0.79 and at 7.5 gives 0.95. Pinning is not better than LRU at the same size.
On the 125B, 20 GB / 2.7 MB is about 7,400 slots, about 15 footprints. LRU already reaches 0.95 or higher there, so the miss rate is about 0.05.
Disk per token is 0.05 x 1.3 GB = 0.065 GB. At 3.1 GB/s that is 21 ms, so the serial bound is 1/(0.021+0.219) = 4.2 tok/s and the overlap bound is 4.57 tok/s. Plain LRU gives the same, minus a few cold tokens.
The one thing pinning adds is a warm start. LRU is cold at the start of decode, and the first tokens run at 0.31 hit at 1 footprint. Prefill warms an LRU for free, since the experts just streamed are already in the cache.
Pinning also has a cost. A static set cannot adapt, so cross-prompt hot lists score only 5-21%, and prefill routing differs from decode routing and is untested.
screened.arithmetic_error: 1) The 3x uses a wrong baseline; 4.6 over 2-4 tok/s is 1.2-2.3x. 2) It assumes zero misses. 3) It never compares against an LRU that prefill warms anyway, so the gain is double counted: the hit rate comes from cache size, not from pinning. 4) It treats "prefill touches most experts" as "the pinned set is exactly what decode needs"; a 20 GB pin holds only about 29% of the experts, and decode hits depend on frequency selection, not on touching. 5) The 8 GB budget is impossible: 1.9 GB dense leaves about 4-5 GB, which is 2 footprints.

screened.idea: Replace the 4.3 bpw expert weights with vector quantisation: each 8-weight block becomes one 8-bit index into a 256-entry codebook, claimed about 1.3 bpw. This cuts expert bytes per token about 3.3x (1.3 GB to 0.39 GB). The 1.9 GB dense part stays resident. It targets decode I/O only, not prefill or the compute ceiling. The brainstorm itself says it needs a fine-tune to recover several % perplexity.
screened.claimed_multiplier: about 3.3x fewer disk bytes per token; brainstorm claims on the family range 1.25x to 16x, with a median around 3x, measured against 2-3 bit scalar quant or mmap
screened.arithmetic: Bytes: 4.3/1.3 = 3.3x. Index alone is 8 bits per 8 weights = 1.0 bpw; a 256x8 fp16 codebook is only 4 KB per tensor, so 1.3 bpw is not derived, only asserted (scales or residual would be needed). Throughput uses the project model, not bytes alone. The decode compute ceiling stays 4.57 tok/s (55 GFLOP/s over 12 GFLOP per token). Experts are about 40% of FLOPs, and a codebook gather adds work, so the ceiling cannot rise and may drop. 8 GB Mac: cache about 4.5 GB. At 4.3 bpw that is 2.1 footprints, hit 0.56, giving 2.18 serial / 4.16 overlap tok/s. At 1.3 bpw a footprint is 0.39 GB, so the cache holds about 11.5 footprints, hit about 0.97, and disk is about 0.01 GB per token. Serial then gives 1/(0.004+0.219) = 4.4 tok/s, a 2.0x gain; overlap gives 4.57, a 1.1x gain. 16 GB: the baseline is already about 8 footprints and hit about 0.93, so about 4.2 tok/s, and the gain is about 1.05x. 32 GB: hit is at least 0.95 and the gain is 1.0x. Against plain mmap at 8 GB (0.53 serial / 0.59 overlap) the same path gives about 8x serial, but about 6x of that is the read-size fix, which our best path already has. A real 2 bpw VQ (AQLM or QuIP# class) gives the same shape: about 4.3/2.0 = 2.15x bytes, about 1.5x at 8 GB serial.
screened.arithmetic_error: 1) Wrong baseline: the 3.3x is against bytes, but the gain over our best path (explicit 4 MiB reads + LRU) is at most 2.0x at 8 GB serial and 1.1x with overlap. 2) Compute bound ignored at 16 GB and above (4.57 tok/s cap, hit already at least 0.93). 3) The 1.3 bpw is asserted: an 8-bit index per 8 weights is 1.0 bpw, and a 256-entry codebook is far too small for 8-dim blocks. QuIP# E8P uses 65,536 entries for 2 bpw, and AQLM 1x16 is 16 bits per 8 weights = 2 bpw. 4) The cache-size effect (more footprints fit) and the byte cut are the same effect and must not be multiplied. 5) Overlap is not implemented. 6) No decode-kernel cost was priced: llama.cpp has no VQ kernel for MoE experts, and a gather-based dequant is likely slower than Q4_K dot products on CPU.

screened.idea: Store every expert as a 2-bit base plus a 2-bit residual enhancement. Keep bases cached or resident; the router's top-4 experts per layer also load the enhancement, so the other experts run at base precision only. The goal is about 2.4x fewer disk bytes per token (0.54 GB vs 1.3 GB), reaching 5-9 tok/s at the 8 GB I/O-bound point. The 32 GB case is claimed to gain from fewer FLOPs.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 2.4x bytes, 5-9 tok/s, "clears 3x"; the claim list contains 1.7 to 36 and the idea text itself says 2.4x
screened.arithmetic:
The idea's own arithmetic does not close. 1.3/0.54 = 2.4x, which is below 3x. A 2-bit base of 69 GB is about 32 GB, not the 24 GB the idea says is 75% resident. The "120 streamed slices" figure is asserted, not derived. A 5-9 tok/s result exceeds the 4.57 tok/s compute ceiling (55 GFLOP/s / 12 GFLOP). Also, 2-bit + 2-bit residual is a 4-bit expert, so enhancement bytes equal the Q4 bytes saved on the base. I replayed the 3 Qwen3-30B traces (run with python3 -I against cachesim.lru_hits). The baseline is a Q4 LRU cache of C entries. The scheme is an LRU of 2C half-size entries (base key plus enhancement key for the first 4 ids of each layer record, assuming the trace order is gate rank, which is optimistic). Bytes per access, Q4 miss rate vs scheme bytes and ratio, for k = cache size in token footprints:
- db: k=2.2: 0.429 -> 0.286 (1.50x); k=4.4: 0.165 -> 0.088 (1.88x); k=8: 0.036 -> 0.029 (1.26x).
- story: k=2.2: 0.385 -> 0.254 (1.52x); k=4.4: 0.131 -> 0.076 (1.72x); k=8: 0.037 -> 0.032 (1.16x).
- code: k=2.2: 0.445 -> 0.311 (1.43x); k=4.4: 0.219 -> 0.121 (1.81x); k=8: 0.061 -> 0.042 (1.46x).
If the enhancement is applied to all 8 ids (top8), the gain is exactly 1.00x, as expected. At k=8 (about 10 GB of cache), Q4 already streams only about 0.05 x 1.3 GB = 0.07 GB per token, which is about 0.02 s at 3 GB/s against 0.22 s of compute, so compute binds and the gain is about 1.0x.
screened.arithmetic_error: (1) Headline 2.4x is below the 3x the idea says it clears. (2) It credits compute savings at 32 GB although decode there is compute-bound and 2-bit kernels do not exist; the idea itself says so. (3) It claims a 5-9 tok/s result, above the 4.57 tok/s compute ceiling. (4) It uses the wrong residency (24/32 = 75% of bases, which leaves 8 GB of bases to stream, not 120 slices). (5) The top-4 enhancement stream (0.24 GB) is added on top of misses without checking for overlap with the missed set. (6) A fixed 75% hit assumption is applied rather than a measured one. (7) The baseline is a pinned or unspecified one, not the Q4 explicit-read plus LRU path. Relative to our best path, the replay gain is 1.4-1.5x at 8 GB.

screened.idea: Turn a second LAN machine into an expert compute server. Split the 512 experts per layer 256/256 between two nodes. Each node streams and multiplies only its own routed experts, then returns about 20 KB of activations per layer. Node 0 keeps the dense part (about 1.9 GB) and the router.
screened.claimed_multiplier: >3x (net 3.5-4 tok/s; compute ceiling 4.6 -> 9.2; traffic 130x smaller than weights)
screened.arithmetic: Traffic: 8 KB hidden state x 10 experts x 48 layers is small, and 10 MB/token is fine. Claimed IO: 0.65 GB/token per node at 2.4 GB/s = 0.27 s = 3.7 tok/s. That uses NO cache, so it ignores the LRU hit that our best path already gets. Compute: the 9.2 ceiling assumes perfect halving. I measured the per-layer straggler on the real traces with a random 50/50 expert split: the busier node does 1.26x its fair share (db 1.258, story 1.280, code 1.250; 8 of 128 experts/layer, 249-299 tokens). The 512-expert model has 10 per layer, so the imbalance is similar or worse. Compute ceiling is therefore 9.14/1.26 = about 7.3 tok/s, not 9.2. Add 48 sequential round trips: 48 x 0.3 ms (GbE) = about 15 ms, so 1/(0.137+0.015) = about 6.6 tok/s overlapped. Pooled RAM, per node (about 3 GB cache each) = 1100 entries / 240 accesses = 4.6 footprints, hit about 0.8. Disk per node is 0.2 x 0.65 x 1.26 = 0.16 GB = 0.07 s. Serial bound: 1/(0.07+0.137+0.015) = 4.5 tok/s. Overlap bound: min(6.6, 14) = 6.6. Versus our best path at 8 GB (2.18 serial / 4.16 overlap): 2.1x serial, 1.6x overlap. screened.idea: Split the expert weights by layer across two machines: the laptop keeps 10 of 48 layers' experts on NVMe, a peer with 16 GB RAM holds the other 38 layers resident. About 79% of the per-token expert bytes (1.03 GB of 1.3 GB) are pulled from the peer's DRAM over RDMA or 25GbE (about 3 GB/s) into a pinned ring. The remaining 21% (0.27 GB) comes from local NVMe. Fetch is pipelined behind compute, and the previous layer's prediction (precision 0.55) prefetches the next layer's peer slices. Claimed result is 2.9 tok/s, rising to 3.3-3.8 tok/s with prefetch, against a 1.2 tok/s baseline.
screened.claimed_multiplier: about 3x (2.9 to 3.8 tok/s over a 1.2 tok/s baseline). Run claims range 1.3 to 3.8x.
screened.arithmetic:
I did not run a script. The check is arithmetic on the measured constants in combo_model.py (LRU curve, 3.11 GB/s explicit reads, 55 GFLOP/s, 1.296 GB of expert bytes per token). Two things were also read from the repo: the corrected 8 GB row in FEED.md, and R18, which I only grepped for network terms.
1) Peer capacity. Expert bytes are about 69 - 1.9 = 67 GB. A 16 GB peer (about 13 GiB usable after OS) holds about 19% of the experts, roughly 9 of 48 layers, not 38. Holding 38 layers (about 53 GB) needs a peer with at least 64 GB of RAM. The idea's own gap list says the same.
2) Baseline. Our best 8 GB path (explicit 4 MiB reads plus LRU, hit 0.56) is 2.18 tok/s serial and 4.16 tok/s overlapped. That is 0.57 GB per token at 2.38 GB/s, which takes 0.24 s. The claim's 1.2 tok/s baseline is weaker than our best path. Its own 2.9 tok/s (0.34 s of I/O) is below our 4.16 overlap row.
3) Fair version with a peer that really has 16 GB. Add about 13 GiB of peer cache to the 2.5 GiB local cache. That is about 12.9 footprints, so combined LRU hit is about 0.96. Of that, 0.56 is local and 0.40 is peer, so 0.52 GB per token crosses the network. At 2.5 GB/s (25GbE practical) that is 0.21 s. Local disk misses are 0.04 x 1.3 GB, about 0.02 s. Compute is 0.219 s at 55 GFLOP/s. Serial: 0.219 + 0.23 = 0.45 s, 2.2 tok/s. Overlap: max(0.22, 0.23), about 4.2 tok/s. This equals the local-NVMe best path (2.18 / 4.16), so the multiplier is about 1.0x. The peer DRAM at about 2.5 GB/s only replaces NVMe at 2.4-3.1 GB/s.
4) Ceiling. The compute ceiling of 4.57 tok/s binds, so no network trick can pass it. 3.8 tok/s is already 83% of it.
5) Layer-predictive prefetch hides at most phi x I/O. At precision 0.55, wasted bytes inflate traffic by 1/0.55 = 1.8x on the network link.
6) Slower links. 10GbE (about 1.1 GB/s) takes 0.47 s for the peer bytes, slower than local NVMe. 1GbE (about 0.11 GB/s) takes 4.7 s per token. Consumer laptops do not have 25GbE or RDMA. Mac RDMA exists only over Thunderbolt 5 on M3 Ultra-class machines.
screened.arithmetic_error: Four errors in the claim. (1) Wrong baseline: 1.2 tok/s is used where our own best path is 2.18 tok/s serial and 4.16 tok/s overlapped. The claimed 2.9-3.8 tok/s is therefore 0.7-0.9x of our best path. (2) Capacity error: 38 of 48 layers is about 53 GB, which does not fit in 16 GB of peer RAM. (3) The 25GbE or RDMA rate of 3 GB/s is assumed. Practical rate is 2.5-2.8 GB/s, and it does not exist on typical small-RAM PCs. (4) It ignores that shipping activations to the peer (layer-split pipeline, a few KB per token) is far cheaper than shipping 1 GB of weights per token. It also ignores the local expert cache, which already supplies 56% of bytes at 8 GB.

real_multiplier.gb32_desktop: 1.0x vs best path. Local cache of 25 GiB gives hit about 0.96 and is compute-bound at 4.57 tok/s. The peer adds nothing.

screened.idea: Split each expert's gate/up/down into column blocks and read only blocks whose SwiGLU intermediate activation is non-negligible (a "zone map" of per-block max activation). Skipped intermediate dims also skip down-matrix rows, so bytes and FLOPs fall together. Claim: 50% dead blocks plus 42% cross-token reuse gives 0.38 GB/token, 6.3 tok/s, 2.6x.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 2.6x (3x+ needs 60% dead blocks); family claims range 1.3x-9x
screened.arithmetic: I recomputed from the stated inputs. 1.3 GB x (1-0.5) x (1-0.42) = 0.377 GB. At 3.1 GB/s that is 0.12 s/token, 8.2 tok/s I/O-only, so the "6.3 tok/s" matches neither that figure nor the compute ceiling. The 1.3 GB base is the no-cache figure (hit 0), so multiplying by (1-0.42) double-counts what an LRU cache already gives. Our best path already reaches about 2.2 tok/s at 8 GB with LRU. The 42% is an expert-level repeat rate, not a block-level hit rate. The traces (qwen3-30b_db/story/code) hold only expert ids, with no activation magnitudes, so the dead fraction cannot be computed from them; I made no new run. The central flaw: h = silu(gate.x) * (up.x) depends on the input, so a static per-block "max activation" zone map cannot say which blocks are dead before the token arrives. To know h you must read gate fully, which is 1/3 of the expert bytes, or use a learned predictor. Gate-first bytes = 1/3 + 2/3 x live. At 50% dead that is 0.667 (1.5x, not 2x). At 60% dead it is 0.60 (1.67x). At a realistic block-level dead fraction of 30% it is 0.80 (1.25x). Compute falls by the same factors; the ceiling goes from 4.57 to about 6.9 tok/s. At 3.1 GB/s, I/O is 2.4 tok/s for the full 1.3 GB and 3.6 tok/s for 0.867 GB, so the overlap bound is 3.6 tok/s, 1.5x at best. The k=8 batching baseline conflicts with this idea: the live-dim union over k tokens grows toward dense (k=8 needs 29.1 unique experts per layer, and live dims behave the same way), so the reuse saving and the sparsity saving cancel each other. Reads also shrink from 2.7 MB extents to column-block fragments (roughly 30 KB per 32 neurons at 4.3 bpw). The measured 3.1 GB/s needs about 2.7 MB reads, and small reads cut throughput, so the effective I/O gain is smaller than the byte cut.
screened.arithmetic_error: (1) Multiplies the 42% reuse into a no-cache 1.3 GB base, which double-counts the LRU/batching baseline. (2) Substitutes an expert-level repeat rate for a block-level hit rate. (3) Assumes a static zone map can identify dead dims, but activations are input-dependent; gate must be read first (1/3 of bytes) or predicted. (4) Ignores small-read throughput loss and the compute ceiling of 4.57 tok/s. (5) 6.3 tok/s does not follow from 0.38 GB at its own stated read rate. (6) The 50% dead fraction at no quality loss is assumed, not measured.

screened.idea: While the user types, run chunked prefill of the live prompt prefix in the background and persist KV (plus warmed experts) keyed by a rolling prefix hash. On send, only the untyped tail is prefilled, so TTFT for a 500-token prompt falls from about 29-109 s to about 1 s. Steady-state decode tok/s is unchanged.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 40x TTFT (claims list 1.3 to 40); the stated goal was 3x or more tokens per second
screened.arithmetic: Cold 500-token prefill: compute is 500 x 12 GFLOP = 6 TFLOP. At the decode-rate 55 GFLOP/s that is 109 s. At the measured batched 311 GFLOP/s it is about 19 s, so the 109 s baseline is already 5.7x too pessimistic. I/O: a 500-token batch touches nearly every expert, so about 69 GB. At 3.1 GB/s that is 22 s, and at mmap 0.34 GB/s it is about 200 s. So realistic cold TTFT is about 22-25 s with explicit reads, because compute and I/O overlap to roughly max(19, 22) s. The 40x only holds if the whole prompt was typed and warmed before send, which is the warm case. A pasted or one-shot prompt gets 1.0x. Incremental chunks (worked example, 25 tokens per chunk): 250 expert draws per layer out of 512 gives about 200 unique experts (about 0.4 of the experts), so about 27 GB per chunk. At 3.1 GB/s that is about 9 s per chunk, and a 500-token prompt is 20 chunks, so about 180 s of total I/O, about 8x more than one batched prefill. These are estimates from the draw model, not yet recomputed on the traces. Typing speed is about 5-10 tok/s at most, so 25 tokens arrive every 3-5 s while a chunk takes 9 s. The background prefill falls behind the typist and competes with decode for the same disk. Only large chunks (about 200 tokens or more) are efficient, and those are only ready after about a minute of typing. Decode tok/s: 0 gain. The ceiling remains 4.57 tok/s.
screened.arithmetic_error: (1) Wrong baseline: 109 s uses the 55 GFLOP/s decode rate, but batched prefill measured 311 GFLOP/s, so 19 s. (2) It ignores that I/O is a separate bound of about 22 s at 3.1 GB/s. (3) The tail is set to 0 by assumption, which is circular for pasted or one-shot prompts. (4) Chunked incremental prefill re-reads most experts per chunk, so total I/O grows about 8x. (5) It is a TTFT lever, not tokens per second. The 1.3x to 10x claims in the list mix up TTFT and decode.

screened.idea: Treat RAM as a per-sequence expert cache (ARC over the active sequence's working set; k=8 union ~29 experts/layer) instead of a global hot list, and add a second machine's RAM over the network (>2.4 GB/s asserted) as the tier for the rest. Claim: bytes/token drop to ~0.4 GB, about 0.17 s, compute-bound at 4.6 tok/s, 1.5-4x.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 1.3x to 4.0x (headline ~1.5-2.3x; 3-3.8x only by stacking 2-bit quantization)
screened.arithmetic: Ran LRU on the 3 Qwen3-30B traces (footprint 384 entries): hit at 1/2/3/4 footprints is db .301/.540/.684/.798, story .326/.585/.734/.839, code .292/.522/.640/.741. So plain LRU, which is already per-sequence (the traces are single sequences), reaches hit ~0.69 at 3 footprints. For the 125B that is 3x480x2.7 MB = 3.9 GB of cache, giving 0.40 GB/token: the same 0.4 GB the idea reaches, with no pinning, no ARC and no network tier. Time at 3.1 GB/s explicit reads = 0.13 s; compute 0.219 s (12/55). Serial 1/(0.13+0.219)=2.9 tok/s; overlap bound min(4.57, 3.1/0.40=7.7)=4.57. The 0.17 s in the claim only holds if the 0.4 GB arrives at ~2.4 GB/s with perfect overlap, which NVMe already gives (3.1 GB/s). The network tier removes no bound: 1 GbE ~0.12 GB/s, 10 GbE ~1.2 GB/s, both below NVMe 3.1 GB/s, and a second machine with RAM for 69 GB is not a small-RAM PC. The 2-bit stacking does not raise the compute ceiling (FLOPs are unchanged by bit width) and duplicates earlier quantization ideas. The 5-21% hot-list vs 42% in-sequence contrast is the known fact that a recency cache beats an offline list (LRU already shows it).
screened.arithmetic_error: (1) Compute-ceiling confusion: 7.6 tok/s from 2-bit is above the 4.57 ceiling and treats FLOPs as scaling with bits. (2) Baseline error: the gain is measured against a cold or global-list cache rather than against LRU at 3 footprints, which already gives the same 0.4 GB/token. (3) The network tier's >2.4 GB/s is unsupported; commodity links are 0.12-1.2 GB/s, so it is slower than local NVMe. (4) Serial and overlap bounds are mixed together.

screened.arithmetic: Recomputed with the 4.57 tok/s compute ceiling and 1.3 GB per token uncached. The claim's 3.8 tok/s is the overlap bound with no cache. The serial figure is 2.1. The claim's own 2.7 comes from adding 0.26 s and 0.22 s, but 1/0.48 is 2.1, not 2.7. The 3.8 figure also assumes full overlap that is not implemented. Our local best path already reads 3.1 GB/s with explicit reads (2.4 GB/s as modelled), so a 5 GB/s remote tier is 1.6x to 2x faster per byte, and only if the link is RDMA-class. The LRU cache applies to both tiers and divides the remote advantage the same way. The top-4 variant gives a compute ceiling of 11.4 tok/s and 0.52 GB per token, but it changes the model, so the quality loss is unmeasured. Without it the cap is 4.57 tok/s.
screened.arithmetic_error: 1) Mixed baseline: it divides by 2.4 GB/s local disk but ignores that our best path reads 3.1 GB/s and has an LRU (hit 0.56 at 2.1 footprints), so the real I/O gain is 1.6x at best. 2) The 2.7 tok/s is internally inconsistent (serial is 2.1, overlap is 3.8). 3) The "top-4 makes 3.8" step is pointless: at 0.26 s I/O the answer is the same 3.8 tok/s, so the top-4 change adds nothing, and the quality cost is unstated. 4) It assumes RDMA at 5 GB/s, which needs Thunderbolt 5 or InfiniBand/RoCE hardware that the target users (8 GB laptop, small-RAM PC) do not have. On a normal LAN of 1 to 10 GbE the rate is 0.12 to 1.15 GB/s, which is slower than the local NVMe at 3.1 GB/s. 5) It needs a second machine with 69+ GB RAM, which contradicts the goal of running on small-RAM PCs. 6) Prefill (first token loads up to ~65 GB) is not covered.

screened.cheapest_test: The decisive number is link bandwidth, which we cannot measure here with the assets we have (no second host on a LAN, no ssh allowed). The free decisive step is arithmetic, already done above: on a 1 to 10GbE LAN the best case is 0.9 to 2.0 tok/s, below the local NVMe path of 2.18/4.16. Only a TB5/RDMA link beats local disk. If someone has such a pair, run: on the server `iperf3 -s`; on the client `iperf3 -c <host> -P 4 -t 10` and then `dd`-style test reading a 1.3 GB range via a 4 MiB-request TCP loop, measure seconds per 1.3 GB. Expected: 10GbE about 1.1 s, TB4 about 0.5 s, RDMA 0.26 s. Kill criterion: if the measured 1.3 GB read takes more than 0.3 s, there is no gain over the local explicit-read path (0.42 s at 3.1 GB/s), and the idea is dead. If it is under 0.3 s, still prefer shipping activations to the remote host (exo/RPC style) over fetching weights.
screened.verdict_reason: Needs a second 69+ GB RAM machine plus an RDMA-class link to reach about 1.6x over our local explicit-read path, and only 3.85 tok/s at the unimplemented overlap bound. On ordinary LANs it is slower than local NVMe (0.09 to 0.9 tok/s uncached). It contradicts the small-RAM goal, and the established alternative (run experts remotely, send activations) already exists in exo and llama.cpp RPC. The top-4 add-on gives no extra speed in its own arithmetic and risks quality.

screened.idea: Set the model's active expert count from 10 to 4 per token and requantise experts to 2-bit. The claim is that bytes and FLOPs both fall 2.5x, so the 4.57 tok/s compute ceiling rises to about 11.5 and the disk bound to about 6.5 tok/s. It needs a finetune to recover quality.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 2.5x on the compute ceiling (4.6 to 11.5 tok/s); claims list up to 32x
screened.arithmetic: Only the routed experts shrink with top-k. 480 slices x 2.7 MB = 1.3 GB per token are experts, and the other 1.9 GB of a roughly 3.2 GB active set is dense. Dense work (attention, shared parts, lm-head) does not shrink. If FLOPs follow active bytes, experts are about 40% of the 12 GFLOP: 4.9 GFLOP expert, 7.1 GFLOP dense. At top-4 the expert part is 0.4 x 4.9 = 1.96, so the total is about 9.1 GFLOP. 55 / 9.1 = 6.0 tok/s, a 1.31x ceiling lift, not 2.5x. This matches our combo model, where top-4 has a marginal effect of x1.23-1.47. The share is derived from byte ratios, not measured FLOPs. Going to 2-bit does not cut FLOPs and adds dequant cost, so it only helps I/O. At 8 GB the best path is 2.18 tok/s serial and 4.16 overlapped. With top-4 there are 192 slices per token, so the same cache holds about 5 footprints and LRU hit rises to about 0.88 (7.5 footprints gives 0.95; 4 gives 0.79). I/O then falls to about 0.06 GB per token, compute binds, and the result is about 5-6 tok/s. That is about 2.4x serial but only 1.3-1.4x against the overlap bound. The 8 GB I/O gain is mostly a bytes/footprint effect, not a compute one.
screened.arithmetic_error: Three errors. (1) It assumes all 12 GFLOP scale with top-k, but about 60% is dense, so the ceiling lift is about 1.3x, not 2.5x. (2) It says the 8 GB I/O bound and the 32 GB compute bound both scale 2.5x, then compounds 2-bit bytes with top-4 bytes as if 2-bit also cut FLOPs. (3) The baseline is the compute ceiling at k=10. It is not our best path (explicit reads + LRU), which already reaches 4.19-4.27 tok/s at 16 and 32 GB. The idea also ignores the compute ceiling for its own 6.5 tok/s I/O figure, and ignores quality and the 2-bit dequant cost.

screened.idea: Per layer, stack the 512 experts' weights, take an SVD to get a shared rank-r basis B (r=64 to start), and keep only a rank-r residual per expert. Each token then computes B·x once per layer and applies a small rank-r residual for each of its 10 routed experts. Bytes and FLOPs per token both fall, which would lift the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling. The claim is conditional on the residual energy being 10% or less at r=64.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 2x to 10x across 9 runs; the idea text claims about 3x, with FLOPs/token of about 0.28 GFLOP vs 12 GFLOP (about 40x fewer FLOPs).
screened.arithmetic:
I did not run SVD, because that needs dequantised weights from the 30B GGUF, which the rules forbid running. This is arithmetic from the idea text and our measured numbers.

(1) The claimed 0.28 GFLOP is 48 x 22 x 64 x 4096. It assumes every expert matrix is replaced by a rank-64 factor pair. For d=4096 and a 125B-class expert (ff about 1.5k to 2k), a full matrix has rank at most min(d, ff), about 1.5k to 2k. So r=64 keeps only about 3 to 4% of the ranks per matrix, and the rest is thrown away. This is a lossy truncation, not "basis + residual".

(2) It is not even a residual scheme: B + rank-r residual is a rank-2r approximation of a full-rank matrix. Any quality loss comes from the discarded tail.

(3) What published methods actually reach at the compression level that keeps quality (MoE-SVD, D2-MoE): 40 to 60% parameter compression, and MoE-SVD reports 1.5x faster inference. That is far from a 40x FLOP cut.

(4) Applying this to our measured bounds, assuming 50% bytes and 50% FLOPs per token (optimistic, with a quality loss unmeasured on our models):
- 8 GB: explicit reads + LRU is 2.18 tok/s serial, so io is 1/2.18 - 1/4.57 = 0.24 s/token and compute is 0.219 s. After the cut: io 0.12 + compute 0.11 = 0.23 s, giving 4.4 tok/s, about 2.0x over our best path. The LRU hit rate would also improve because the cache holds twice as many experts, which adds a little more.

(4) k=8 grouping alone gives 0.453x bytes (2.2x), but the first screen already found no gain once an LRU of 2-4 footprints exists. The 8.7x is 3.93 x 2.2 with an unsupported 3.93. (5) The base expert for layer L is a layer L-1 expert that must be resident or read. So the idea's 14 s and 109 s both come from using the decode rate for prefill. Our measured batched prefill rate is 311 GFLOP/s, which gives 2.5 s for block 1 and 19.3 s for all 500 tokens. The compute-bound full prefill is therefore about 19 s, not 109 s. The real prefill bottleneck is I/O. A 64-token block with uniform top-10 routing over 512 experts touches about 367 of 512 experts per layer (72%), so about 49 GB of expert bytes. At 3.1 GB/s that is about 16 s for block 1 alone. A 500-token prompt touches 512/512 experts (all 69 GB, 22 s or more). Real routing is more clustered than uniform, so these are upper estimates, and no prefill trace exists. So block 1 cannot appear at about 14 s from compute, and it is not cheaper than the whole prompt in bytes. Block 1 already costs about 70% of the full read, so the 6-8x is not available. A second problem is that prefill produces no output. Output tokens exist only after the prompt is fully consumed, so streaming from block 1 means generating from a truncated prompt (the last 436 prompt tokens are unseen). That is a guess about the answer, not progress on it. The 'idle decode slots' do not exist either. The CPU is the bottleneck at 55-311 GFLOP/s, and every provisional decode token (12 GFLOP) and every verify pass steals compute from the prefill it overlaps. The 6-8x also divides time-to-first-token by the end-of-completion time, which are different metrics.

screened.arithmetic: Compute part is right: 32 x 12 / 311 = 1.23 s, 0.038 s/token, about 26 tok/s. But it drops I/O. Verifying k tokens reads the union of their experts. I modelled it as: bytes per token = 1.3 GB x (u/8) x (1-hit) / k, read at 3.1 GB/s, plus 0.039 s compute. With 100% acceptance and the same hit rate, verify cost is 0.18 s/token at 8 GB (k=8; 0.23 s at k=4), 0.12 s at 16 GB, 0.077 s at 32 GB. I took baseline decode as our best path: 2.18, 3.0 and 4.2 tok/s. With a fraction f of tokens emitted via spans, speedup = baseline time / ((1-f) x baseline + f x verify). screened.idea: Run chunked prefill on the partial prompt while the user is still typing, reusing the exact causal-prefix KV, so only the last chunk (about 64 tokens, about 14 s) remains at Enter instead of 109 s. Optionally also stream a draft answer from early chunks and revise it as later chunks arrive. This is latency hiding for time-to-first-token (TTFT). It leaves decode tokens per second unchanged.
screened.claimed_multiplier: Perceived speed up 3-4x (TTFT 109 s to about 14 s, about 7.8x on TTFT only). No tok/s figure is derived from the given numbers.
screened.arithmetic: Only the arithmetic from the facts you supplied; I ran no trace computation, because none of the traces can test the claim (they are decode-only). Decode ceiling stays 55 GFLOP/s / 12 GFLOP = 4.57 tok/s, and the idea touches neither FLOPs per token nor bytes per token. The ratio 109 s / 14 s = 7.8x is a TTFT ratio, not tok/s. The claim of '3-4x perceived tok/s' has no derivation. The idea also assumes the typing window is long enough. At typing speed of about 1-3 tokens/s, a 64-token chunk fills in 20-60 s. Each chunk pass must stream most of the 512 experts per layer from disk, because a 64-token chunk covers nearly every expert (k=8 consecutive tokens already need 29.1 of 64 slots, and 64 tokens saturate it). At 3.1 GB/s that is about 65 GB / 3.1 = 21 s per chunk pass, and 69 GB does not fit in 8-32 GB RAM. So chunking during typing costs one full weight read per chunk, which is more disk work than a single big prefill pass. Expert reads for typing-time chunks also evict the decode cache, so decode after Enter starts cold (LRU hit 0.0 at the start). The 14 s tail-chunk figure is therefore at best the compute time. With I/O it is about 21 s or more. For pasted prompts, which are the long ones, there is no typing window at all, so TTFT stays 109 s.
screened.arithmetic_error: Category error: a TTFT/latency shift is counted as a tok/s multiplier ('perceived 3-4x'). Hidden assumption that typing time is free: prefill competes for the same disk and RAM, and the cache is cold again after the prompt. The 14 s tail chunk is compute only and omits the weight read of about 21 s per chunk at 3.1 GB/s. The draft-and-revise stream is a quality risk with no measured acceptance.

screened.idea: Claim: the 55 GFLOP/s decode and 311 GFLOP/s prefill rates are dispatch-overhead artifacts. Ahead-of-time specialise the fixed 48-layer, 10-of-512 structure into fused, unrolled, pre-gathered kernels, which would cut about 60% of the 109 s prefill and bring TTFT to about 45 s (2.4x), with bit-identical math.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 2.4x TTFT (109 s to 45 s); the family text also implies 6-9 tok/s by stacking on the read path
screened.arithmetic:
I did not run the traces. The idea does not touch routing or I/O, so they cannot test it. I recomputed from the stated structure.

1. The 55 and 311 GFLOP/s figures are achieved rates, measured on the real ggml path with its dispatch already included. A 60% overhead share would mean the kernels run at 2.5x the measured rate. Nothing measured shows this.
2. Launch count: ggml's MUL_MAT_ID is one graph op per matrix per layer, and the expert loop runs inside it. That is 3 matrices x 48 layers = 144 ops per token, not 23k launches. Even counting 480 x 3 = 1,440 slice-matmuls per token at 2-5 us each gives 3-7 ms.
3. Decode time per token is 1/4.6 = 217 ms, so dispatch is about 1-3% of decode.
4. Prefill: a batch groups tokens by expert, so there are at most 512 x 3 x 48 = 74k expert-matmuls per pass. At 10 us each that is 0.7 s of 109 s, under 1%. The 109 s is arithmetic: 311 GFLOP/s x 109 s = about 34 TFLOP, which matches roughly 2.8k prompt tokens x 12 GFLOP. It is compute-bound.
5. Real headroom is in the kernel's arithmetic efficiency, such as better Q4 dot kernels or AMX/NEON i8mm. That is known work and it is not "dispatch". A 4-core CPU peaks at roughly 100-200 GFLOP/s fp32 per core-cluster. Gains of 1.2-1.5x in prefill are plausible from better quantised GEMM, not 2.4x from removing dispatch.
6. Double count: the idea removes 60% from a rate that already includes the overhead, and also keeps 29 s of overlapped I/O. It also does nothing for decode, which is I/O-bound at 1.30 GB/token and 3.1 GB/s, about 2.4 tok/s I/O-limited, below the 4.57 compute ceiling. Even a perfect fix of the compute ceiling would not change decode at 8-16 GB.
screened.arithmetic_error: 1) The 55 and 311 GFLOP/s figures are measured achieved rates, so removing a "60% overhead" from them double-counts. 2) The launch count is wrong: 23k comes from 480 slices x 48 layers, but ggml issues about 144 graph ops per token, with the expert loop inside the op, and launching is cheap on a CPU. 3) A prefill speedup is stacked onto a decode claim. 4) It ignores that decode is I/O-bound (1.30 GB/token over 3.1 GB/s gives 2.4 tok/s), so the compute ceiling is not the binding limit.

screened.idea: Use grammar/schema-constrained decoding with jump-forward (fast-forward) tokens: when the grammar leaves one legal token, append it without sampling, so forced runs ride along in the next forward instead of costing one forward each. The claim is that at f=0.7 of output tokens forced, forwards per output token drop to 0.3, giving more than 3x (2-4 to 6.7-13 tok/s).
screened.arithmetic: I ran a model from our numbers. Forward cost is I/O 1.3 GB x (unique experts / 8) / 3.1 GB/s, plus compute at 55 GFLOP/s (batch 1) or 311 GFLOP/s (batch > 1). That gives 0.42 s I/O + 0.22 s compute for one token. Batches of k tokens cost 0.66 s (k=2), 0.85 s (k=3), 1.03 s (k=4) and 1.53 s (k=8) with I/O and compute overlapped (0.97 s at k=3 and 1.18 s at k=4 serial), because unique experts per layer grow 12.6 / 16.3 / 19.6 / 29.1. Forced tokens are not free. They still need KV entries and expert outputs, so they cost a batched forward. The saving is only the part of the I/O that overlaps across the batch. Per output token, with I/O bound and a cold cache: f=0.3 with runs of 2 gives 1.17x; f=0.5 with runs of 3 gives 1.35x; f=0.7 with runs of 3 gives 1.57x; f=0.7 with runs of 7 gives 1.77x. The hard ceiling at f=0.7 is about 2.7x, reached only if forced runs are infinitely long and cost the prefill rate of 311 GFLOP/s (26 tok/s). The ceiling is therefore 1/(0.3 + 0.7 x 0.1), not 3.3x.
screened.arithmetic_error: There are three errors. (1) It treats forced tokens as zero cost. They still need a forward over their positions (KV and hidden states), as the LMSYS and XGrammar sources say they are prefilled. (2) It ignores that a batched forward touches more unique experts: 19.6 per layer for 4 tokens versus 8 for one. (3) f=0.7 is unsupported. Value tokens dominate real JSON output, and the idea's own gaps list says so. There is also a denominator redefinition: output tokens of a schema are counted, including template tokens the user did not need generated. It is an application-level speedup that only applies when a schema is known, not a decode-rate gain.

real_multiplier.gb8_laptop: about 1.1-1.3x on schema-constrained output at f=0.2-0.4, and 1.0x (nothing) on free text. Relative to our best path (explicit reads + LRU, 2.18 serial / 4.16 overlap tok/s), where cache hit ~0.26-0.56.
real_multiplier.gb16_laptop: about 1.1-1.4x on schema output; the gain is larger when compute dominates, because forced tokens are batched at 311 GFLOP/s instead of 55. Free text 1.0x.
real_multiplier.gb32_desktop: about 1.2-1.6x on schema output, up to about 2.7x only at f=0.7 with long forced runs. Free text 1.0x.
real_multiplier.bound: 1/((1-f) + f x c), where c is the batched cost of a forced token relative to a normal one. c is about 0.1-0.4 (compute 12 GFLOP at 311 GFLOP/s plus extra unique experts). That gives at most 2.7x at f=0.7 and about 1.2-1.5x at realistic f. No effect on free text.
real_multiplier.vs: our best path (explicit large reads + LRU); the same ratio applies on top of plain mmap since it multiplies tokens per forward

screened.quality_risk: Low for forced tokens in principle, since the tokens are exactly the grammar-determined ones. Two risks. Second, constraining output to a schema can reduce quality, and it only applies when a schema is known. The speedup does not apply to the main use case (free-form reasoning and prose).

screened.novelty_reason: Jump-forward / fast-forward decoding has been published and shipped since 2023-24 in SGLang, XGrammar, and llguidance (which llama.cpp can use). The idea's "no forward pass" wording is also wrong, because the forced tokens are prefilled.
screened.cheapest_test: Measure f and run lengths, not model speed. Build a tokenizer-only measurement using llama-tokenize (vocab only, no model run) or a Python tokenizer. Take 20 real schema outputs (JSON from our MCP planner/verifier, tool calls) and a JSON-schema grammar. Simulate the grammar automaton token by token and count (a) f = forced tokens / total tokens and (b) the histogram of forced-run lengths L. Plug f and L into the cost model above (batched forward costs 0.66 / 0.85 / 1.03 / 1.53 s for k = 2 / 3 / 4 / 8 against 0.42-0.64 s for k = 1). Expected result: f 0.2-0.4, mean L 2-3, giving 1.1-1.4x. Kill criterion: if f < 0.5 or mean L < 3 on our real workload, drop it; if f >= 0.65 with L >= 3, the multiplier is at most about 1.6x and it is still not a several-times lever. Optionally validate the batch cost with the existing router traces: count unique experts for 2-8 consecutive tokens with cachesim.py/trace_tools.py on data/traces/qwen3-30b_*.txt (expected 12.6 / 16.3 / 19.6 / 29.1 of 8 per token).
screened.verdict_reason: It is known prior art (jump-forward / fast-forward in SGLang, XGrammar and llguidance). Forced tokens are batched, not free, and the extra unique experts they touch cap the multiplier at about 1.2-1.6x for realistic f. It does nothing for free text. It can be bolted onto the planner's JSON outputs through llguidance only if we need schema output, and it is not a several-times lever.

screened.idea: Store each expert as a 2-bit base plus 4-bit refinement tiles (about 6 bits stored). Read and compute the base for all 480 routed slices per token, and read the refinement tile only for slices whose residual norm exceeds a threshold. The claim is that per-token bytes fall from 1.3 GB to about 0.72 GB (about 0.60 base + 0.12 refinement if 10% or fewer slices refine), giving 3.3-4.2 tok/s at 8 GB.
screened.claimed_multiplier: 3x+ (3.3-4.2 tok/s) at 8 GB; the idea itself says none at 32 GB
screened.arithmetic: Ran the LRU curve from combo_model.py: 4.3 bpw, 1.296 GB/token, 2.4 GB/s explicit reads, ceiling 4.57 tok/s, 8 GB cache 2.7 GB. (1) Our best path (explicit reads + 4-bit LRU) at 8 GB: 2.19 tok/s serial, 4.20 overlap, hit 0.56. This matches the FEED corrected row (2.18/4.16). (2) Idea with a base-only cache (2.2 bpw, 0.66 GB per token, so the cache holds about 4.1 footprints, hit 0.795) and refinement of 10% of slices only on misses: 3.5-3.6 tok/s serial, which is 1.6x vs 2.19. Overlap is capped at 4.57, which is 1.09x vs 4.20. (3) If the refinement tiles are re-read every token because they are not cached (this is what the idea literally describes): 3.07 tok/s serial, 1.4x. (4) 16 GB: 4-bit already 4.07 serial / 4.57 overlap; idea 4.32-4.36 serial, 1.06-1.07x. (5) 32 GB: 4.18 -> 4.32-4.36, 1.03-1.04x. The "3x" appears only against plain mmap (0.53 serial at 8 GB), and that gap is the read-size gain, which our path already has. Files are 6 bpw stored (about 97 GB for the 125B vs 69 GB), so the cache footprint of base+refined slices is larger than the 4-bit footprint if refined tiles are cached too.
screened.arithmetic_error: (a) Wrong baseline: the 1.3 GB/token is the zero-hit figure; at 8 GB our LRU already misses only 44%, so the real baseline is 0.57 GB/token, not 1.3 GB. (b) The byte cut and the bandwidth rate are mixed: 0.96 GB at 2.4 GB/s is 2.5 tok/s, then 3.3-4.2 tok/s is reached by also using the 3 GB/s figure, which counts the faster read twice (it is the same large-read gain already in the baseline). (c) The refinement is not free: the base pass reads all 480 slices and the refinement tiles are extra scattered reads. (d) "Slices exceeding a residual threshold" is a weight property if static (then it is just a per-slice mixed-precision map, which is a known idea), or needs a per-token activation test that is not defined. A per-token decision cannot be made before the base bytes are read, so it adds latency. (e) Ignored the 4.57 compute ceiling in the overlap case, and the 2-bit dequant does not raise FLOPs/s (the 55 GFLOP/s is unchanged). (f) The 2-bit base quality loss and the 6 bpw storage growth (about 1.4x file) are not priced.

real_multiplier.gb8_laptop: 1.4-1.6x serial (2.19 -> 3.1-3.6 tok/s), 1.09x overlap (4.20 -> 4.57 cap); about 6-7x vs plain mmap but that is read size, not this idea
real_multiplier.gb16_laptop: 1.06-1.07x (4.07 -> 4.32-4.36 serial; overlap already at the cap)
real_multiplier.bound: Compute ceiling 4.57 tok/s (55 GFLOP/s / 12 GFLOP). 2-bit does not change FLOPs. 8 GB gain needs the 2-bit base cache to hold about 4 footprints (hit 0.795 from the measured LRU curve).
real_multiplier.vs: our best path (explicit 2.7 MB reads + LRU, 4-bit)

screened.quality_risk: High. A 2-bit base is used as the compute path for most slices; unrefined slices carry 2-bit error (Eliseev and Mazur saw the biggest MMLU drop near 2.6 bpw). Perplexity and KL on the 125B were never measured. The residual-threshold rule has no accuracy evidence. The 6 bpw stored format also grows the file to about 97 GB, which does not fit the Mac disk (54-57 GB free) and costs install time.
