screened.cheapest_test: Step 1 (free, local, no model run): cachesim bytes test. Command: python3 -I -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'<tinyram-llm>/tools');import trace_tools,cachesim;..." Parse the three Qwen3-30B traces with trace_tools.parse, build accesses, and use cachesim.lru_hits(accesses, cap) at cap = cache_bytes / slice_bytes for slice bytes 2.2 bpw vs 4.3 bpw (cap ratio 1.95x), at 2.5/9.15/25.15 GiB scaled to the 384-slice footprint. Measure hit rate and tok/s = 1/((1-h)*bytes/2.4e9 + 1/4.57). Expected: at 8 GB hit rises 0.56 -> 0.79, serial 2.19 -> about 3.5 tok/s (1.6x); at 16/32 GB at most 1.07x. Kill: if the 8 GB serial gain over the 4-bit LRU is under 1.5x, or the 16 GB gain under 1.1x, the idea is an 8 GB-only trick equal to plain 2-bit. Step 2 (reads weights only, needs permission, not a model run): read 3 expert tensors of ~/Downloads/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Q4_K_M.gguf with the gguf python package, requantise to a 2-bit-class format, and compute relative residual norm per 32-weight group and per expert slice. Measure the fraction of slices above a threshold that keeps the output error (on a random activation) under that of Q4_K. Kill: more than 10% of slices need refinement, or the residual norm is spread evenly (coefficient of variation under 0.2), in which case there is nothing to select. Step 3 (model run, later): llama-perplexity on OLMoE with Q2_K vs Q4_K; kill above +5% perplexity.
screened.verdict_reason: It is a variant of the already closed mixed-bit expert idea, with the prior art above (HOBBIT, 2512.17073, Any-Precision LLM). The 3x claim uses a plain-mmap or zero-hit baseline plus a double-counted bandwidth. Against our best path the gain is 1.4-1.6x serial and 1.09x overlap at 8 GB, and 1.03-1.07x at 16-32 GB, because the 4.57 tok/s compute ceiling binds. It also adds 6 bpw storage and an undefined residual trigger. Keep only as an 8 GB fallback folded into the low-bit and HOBBIT-style miss-precision lever behind a perplexity gate.

ranked.summary: 26 screenings merged into 16 mechanisms. Ten of them have a real tok/s effect or are compute-ceiling lifters, and they are ranked below. The other six groups are in `dropped`. No candidate qualifies as revolutionary. Only one reaches 3x or more over our best path (layer skipping at 67% of layers). It is published, and its quality cost is unsupported. Every other idea lands at 1.0-2.1x against our best path (explicit large reads + LRU: 2.18 serial / 4.16 overlap tok/s at 8 GB, about 4.19 and 4.27 at 16 and 32 GB). The compute ceiling of 4.57 tok/s (55 GFLOP/s / 12 GFLOP per token) binds at 16 and 32 GB. Only compute-ceiling lifters matter there. The I/O-only ideas (prefetch, cache policy, peer RAM, delta, base+refinement) cap at about 1.0-1.1x at those sizes.

candidates.idea: Layer skipping (early exit / router-chosen layers): run about 16 of 48 layers per token. This is a pure FLOP and byte lifter of the compute ceiling.
candidates.real_multiplier: Arithmetic only, from combo_model.py at 33% of layers kept: 8 GB 4.65x serial / 5.1x overlap, 16 GB 3.1x / 3.2x, 32 GB 3.0x / 3.15x. At 50% kept: 2.7x / 2.0x / 2.0x. At 75% kept: 1.5x / 1.4x / 1.3x. At 16 and 32 GB it is exactly 1/fraction of the compute ceiling. The screener calls the 8 GB 4.65x overstated (about 3x is honest). The screener's realistic, quality-preserving range is 10-25% skipped, which gives about 1.1-1.4x.
candidates.prior_art: Dr.LLM (2510.12773, about 5 layers skipped per example, not MoE), LayerSkip (Meta, ACL 2024, needs training, 1.8-2.2x), ShortGPT (2403.03853, about 25% removal costs MMLU 55.0 to 52.2). Qwen3-MoE reportedly defers decisions to deep layers (secondary source, unverified). Our combo_model.py already has an 'exit' lever.
candidates.test: Step 1 is free: per-layer-pair expert-set Jaccard on the three Qwen3-30B traces. Step 2 is decisive and needs a model run: llama-perplexity with 25%, 50% and 67% of layers masked. Kill if PPL at 50% skipped rises by more than 15%, or 67% skipped is above 2x baseline PPL.
candidates.test_cost: cheap-local-run (step 1 is free; step 2 is a model run)
candidates.why_ranked_here: It is the only idea whose arithmetic reaches 3x or more over our best path, and it is a compute-ceiling lifter. It is ranked first on arithmetic, not on credibility. It is published, and the 67% skip ratio has no supporting evidence. It does not qualify as revolutionary.

candidates.idea: Multi-node expert-parallel decode: split the 512 experts 256/256 across two LAN machines and ship about 20 KB of activations per layer. This is a compute-ceiling lifter, but it needs a second machine.
candidates.real_multiplier: Straggler measured on real traces at 1.25-1.28x, so the compute ceiling is about 7.3 tok/s (not 9.2). With 48 round trips (about 15 ms) the overlap bound is about 6.6 tok/s. Vs our best path: 8 GB about 2.1x serial / 1.6x overlap; 16 and 32 GB about 1.4-1.45x. The bound is N/1.26 on compute: 1.59x for two nodes, 3.2x for four nodes. That needs N machines.
candidates.prior_art: OD-MoE (2512.03927), latency-optimized expert placement (2508.12851), inter-layer expert affinity (2401.08383), exo on 8 Mac Minis (5.37 tok/s for 671B), llama.cpp RPC.
candidates.test: Free: replay the three traces with 20 random seeds plus a balanced split to measure the straggler, then run cachesim LRU per half-stream. Drop if the best balanced straggler is above 1.15 or the modelled 8 GB gain is below 1.5x. A real test needs two machines and a timed RPC round trip (abandon if 48 round trips exceed 40 ms).
candidates.why_ranked_here: It is the highest realistic multiplier that preserves exact output (1.4-2.1x). It is a compute-ceiling lifter, but each machine's own gain is below 1 and it is known work. It is optional on top of the single-node path.

candidates.idea: Reduce active experts from 10 to 4 (top-k) and add 2-bit expert quantisation. The top-k half lifts the compute ceiling.
candidates.real_multiplier: Only about 40% of the 12 GFLOP is experts (4.9 expert, 7.1 dense). At top-4 the total is about 9.1 GFLOP, so the ceiling is about 6.0 tok/s (1.31x), not 11.5. Vs our best path: 8 GB about 2.4x serial but 1.3-1.4x vs overlap (hit rises to about 0.88 with 192 slices per token); 16 and 32 GB about 1.4x (4.19 and 4.27 to about 6.0). The 2-bit half adds nothing to FLOPs. Quality is unmeasured and likely poor without a finetune.
candidates.prior_art: NAEE (2402.14800), LExI (2509.02753), HookMoE (1.42x prefill), MC-MoE (top-k reduction plus 2-bit, with code), vllm-mlx --moe-top-k (Qwen3-30B-A3B top-8 to top-4: +16.5% decode at 4-bit, +24% at 3-bit with broken output), a Qwen 3.5 122B 8-to-4 post (with retraining), and our own R16 screen (verdict: combine-with-other).
candidates.test: llama-perplexity and llama-bench on OLMoE with --override-kv expert_used_count = 8, 4, 2, plus a Q2_K variant. Kill if the speedup at half k is below 1.5x (already predicted) or PPL rises more than 5% at the planned k.
candidates.why_ranked_here: It is a compute-ceiling lifter, but the real lift is 1.3x because the dense share is fixed. It is quality-gated, and it is a variant of the top-k and mixed-bit families already screened.

candidates.idea: Shared low-rank basis per layer with per-expert residuals. This merges the shared-basis/residual idea with the rank-64 SVD idea.
candidates.real_multiplier: The two screenings disagree on compute. idx5 says compute is untouched (extra basis matmuls) and the gain is about 1.3x serial / 1.1x overlap at 8 GB and 1.0x at 32 GB, with 2-3 bit residuals giving at most 1.7x fewer bytes, not 3.6x. idx17 assumes an optimistic 50% bytes and 50% FLOPs: 8 GB about 1.5-2x, 16 and 32 GB about 1.3-1.7x. Published methods reach only 40-60% compression (MoE-SVD about 1.5x faster, MoBE 24-30% parameter cut). The combo model rates low-rank at x0.86-0.98. The 40x FLOP claim is dead.
candidates.prior_art: D2-MoE (ICML 2025, 2502.17298), MoE-SVD (ICML 2025), MoBE (2508.05257), Sub-MoE (2506.23266), DeltaMoE (2.34x compression), RFID-MoE, low-rank compensation for offloaded MoE (2512.17073).
candidates.test: One-layer weight SVD with the gguf python package: residual energy after mean removal, and rank 16/64/256 energy. Kill if residual energy at r=64 is above 20%, or the byte ratio needed to match Q4 error is above 0.45.
candidates.why_ranked_here: It is a possible compute lifter (only idx17's version) of about 1.3-2x. Quality is unmeasured, it needs ggml kernel work, and it is heavily published.

candidates.idea: Intra-expert activation sparsity ('zone map' of dead SwiGLU blocks): read and compute only the live column blocks. Byte and FLOP lifter.
candidates.real_multiplier: A static map cannot predict input-dependent activations. Reading the gate first costs 1/3 of the bytes, so the bytes factor is 1/3+2/3*(1-d). That is 1.5x at d=0.5, 1.67x at d=0.6 and 1.25x at d=0.3. The compute ceiling could go from 4.57 to about 6.9. Net vs our best path: 8 GB 1.0-1.3x, 16 GB 1.1-1.4x, 32 GB 1.0-1.2x. Small block reads (about 30 KB) cut disk throughput, and k-token batching erases the sparsity.
candidates.prior_art: TEAL (ICLR 2025, 40-50% sparsity, 1.53-1.8x on dense models), FloE (2505.05950), PowerInfer-2, LLM in a flash, TurboSparse/dReLU (needs retraining), DualSparse-MoE, CATS.
candidates.test: Dump ffn_moe_swiglu on OLMoE for 100 tokens and measure the byte-weighted dead fraction at block 32 and 2% output error. Kill if d is below 0.55 or the k=8 union dead fraction is below 0.3.
candidates.why_ranked_here: A genuine compute-ceiling lifter in principle, but gate-first reading caps it at about 1.5x, quality is unmeasured, and it is well published.

candidates.idea: Vector quantisation of experts (8-weight blocks as codebook indices), optionally with a LUT-gather matmul kernel. This merges the 2.4 bpw LUT idea with the 1.3 bpw VQ idea.
candidates.real_multiplier: Bytes only (idx2, 2.4 bpw): 4.3/2.4 = 1.79x, not about 3x. 8 GB gives about 1.5x serial / 1.1x overlap, and 16 and 32 GB give 1.0x. idx8 (1.3 bpw) gives at most 2.0x serial / 1.1x overlap at 8 GB and 1.0x at 32 GB. Its 1.3 bpw is not derived (an 8-bit index per 8 weights is 1.0 bpw), and quality is unlikely to survive. A real 2 bpw VQ gives about 1.5x serial. LUT-kernel compute half (idx2): 0.7-1.5x of the current int8 dot kernel, so the ceiling lifts to about 6.9 tok/s at best. 8x ops or 37 tok/s is not credible.
candidates.prior_art: T-MAC (2407.00088, LUT kernels, gains largest at 1-2 bit against weak dequant baselines), AQLM with CPU LUT kernels (2401.06118, gains against FP32), KBVQ-MoE (ICLR 2026, near-FP16 at 3 bit), QMoE, MoQE, VPTQ, GPTVQ, llama.cpp IQ2 codebook quants.
candidates.test: Microbenchmark lutbench.c: LUT-gather GEMV vs int8 dot on an expert-sized matrix (768x2048) on an x86 AVX2 box. Kill if the LUT kernel is below 2x the dot kernel. For the bytes half, a k-means VQ error test on one Qwen3-30B tensor against Q2_K error.
candidates.why_ranked_here: The bytes part is the already-modelled bpw lever, worth 1.0x at 16 and 32 GB. Only the LUT kernel is a compute lifter, and it is unproven (0.7-1.5x), known, and quality-risky.

candidates.idea: Prompt-lookup / suffix-automaton n-gram speculation: draft spans from the context and verify them in one batched pass. Verified tokens run at the batched rate, so this partly lifts the compute ceiling.
candidates.real_multiplier: Verify I/O is not free: unique experts per layer are 12.6 / 16.3 / 19.6 / 29.1 for k = 2 / 3 / 4 / 8, so bytes per token fall to at most 0.45x. Typical gain is 1.05-1.3x. With about 60% of tokens from spans and full acceptance it reaches 1.5-1.7x. 3x needs f above 0.9 and 100% acceptance. The 8 GB baseline is 2.18, not 4.6.
candidates.prior_art: Prompt Lookup Decoding and llama.cpp lookup / --spec-type ngram-cache, SAM Decoding (2411.10666, 2.27x on dense models), MoE-Spec/EVICT/AcceptMoE (verify cost grows with draft size on MoE).
candidates.test: Measure the accepted-token fraction f with a greedy suffix match on saved outputs. Replay k=8 windows through cachesim LRU at 2.1 footprints. Kill if the modelled gain is below 1.3x at measured f, or f_accepted is below 0.3 on chat or story text.
candidates.why_ranked_here: Lossless and already in llama.cpp, but it only helps repetitive output (1.05-1.3x typical). It is a partial compute lifter limited by verify-pass I/O.

candidates.idea: Grammar-constrained jump-forward decoding: batch the forced tokens in one forward pass. Applies only when a schema is known.
candidates.real_multiplier: Forced tokens still cost a batched forward and touch more experts. Realistic schema output is 1.1-1.4x. The hard ceiling at f=0.7 is about 2.7x, not 3.3x, and only with infinitely long forced runs. Free text is 1.0x.
candidates.prior_art: SGLang compressed FSM / jump-forward (2024), XGrammar (2411.15100), llguidance fast-forward tokens (usable from llama.cpp), Formatron.
candidates.test: Tokenizer-only measurement: simulate the grammar automaton on 20 real schema outputs and measure f and the forced-run length histogram. Drop if f is below 0.5 or mean run length is below 3.
candidates.why_ranked_here: It raises throughput through batching, but only for structured output and capped at about 1.2-1.6x at realistic f. It is already shipped elsewhere.

candidates.idea: Low-bit base (2-bit) plus selective refinement tiles / top-4 enhancement. This merges the two base+refinement ideas.
candidates.real_multiplier: idx9 trace replay: bytes per access improve 1.4-1.5x at 2.1 footprints, up to 1.88x at 4.4, and 1.0x if the enhancement covers all 8 ids. Realistic 8 GB tok/s gain is 1.0-1.3x (two smaller reads lower the disk rate). speed5 gives 1.4-1.6x serial / 1.09x overlap at 8 GB, 1.06-1.07x at 16 GB and 1.03-1.04x at 32 GB. The stored size is about 6 bpw (about 97 GB for the 125B). The claimed 5-9 tok/s exceeds the 4.57 ceiling.
candidates.prior_art: HOBBIT (2411.01433, llama.cpp-based, up to 9.93x vs offload baselines), D2MoE nested MWQ (2504.15299), Matryoshka Quantization, Any-Precision LLM, DynaExq, low-rank compensation (2512.17073).
candidates.test: cachesim replay at 2.2 vs 4.3 bpw footprints (free), then an OLMoE PPL run with a Q2_K base. Kill if the 8 GB serial gain is under 1.5x or PPL rises more than 5%.
candidates.why_ranked_here: An I/O-only lever that helps at 8 GB and nothing at 16 and 32 GB. Known and quality-gated.

dropped: Computational-storage FPGA drives for expert GEMV (idx1): about 1.1x vs overlapped best path (2.1x serial). Per-drive flash read of 0.65 GB at about 3 GB/s gives 0.22 s, equal to the compute floor and to striping two plain NVMe drives. Laptops have no such drives, and no GEMV numbers exist. partly-known (InstInfer and HillInfer offload KV and attention, not experts). Free test: striping arithmetic.

Cache policy: prefill-warmed pinning (idx7) and per-sequence ARC plus network tier (idx14). About 1.0-1.1x, because prefill-warmed LRU gets the same hit rate (29% pinned gives 0.81-0.87, LRU at the same size is similar). Pinning only fixes cold start. A network tier is slower than local NVMe. Known: SeqMoE (PrefillHot), MoE-Infinity, DAOP, llama.cpp issue 20757.

Cross-layer expert prefetch (idx4): 1.00-1.07x at 8 GB and 1.0x at 16 and 32 GB on held-out traces, from an event simulation. Held-out precision is 0.31-0.43, not 0.55. The lead time is one layer (about 4.6 ms), not a token. Known: Fate, ProMoE, HOBBIT. Flash-MoE logged prefetch as net 0%.

Peer-RAM weight fetch over RDMA/25GbE/100GbE (idx11, idx15, idx18, same mechanism): about 1.0x vs best path, 1.1x overlap and 1.5-1.7x serial at 8 GB only with a 100GbE or TB5 link and a 69 GB-RAM peer. On 1-10 GbE it is slower than local NVMe (0.09-0.9 tok/s uncached). The 4.57 tok/s ceiling still binds. Shipping activations (llama.cpp RPC, exo) beats shipping weights. partly-known / known. A 16 GB peer holds about 9 layers, not 38.

Cross-layer expert delta (idx19): about 1.0x (0.9-1.0). Bound is 1.7x even with a 4x residual, because only 55% of slices are predicted. Cross-layer weights are near-orthogonal and lossless compression measured 1.03x. partly-known; free weight-correlation test would likely kill it.

AOT-specialised fused kernels (r7 idx3): dispatch is about 1-3% of decode and under 1% of prefill. The measured 55 and 311 GFLOP/s already include dispatch. Real prefill headroom is better quantised GEMM (KTransformers, ik_llama.cpp), a separate known lever. About 1.0-1.1x.

TTFT-only ideas, with 0x tok/s effect by their own statement: NPU/FPGA prefill co-processor (idx0, about 1.0x TTFT because prefill is already I/O-bound at 22-44 s vs 19 s compute); persisted prefix KV (idx3, 40-50x TTFT on an exact hit, 1.0x on a miss, but stock llama.cpp --prompt-cache and slot save/restore); typing-time chunked prefill (idx13 + r7 idx2, same mechanism; best case 5-10x TTFT on typed prompts with idle disk, but chunking re-reads about 8x the expert bytes and pasted prompts get 1.0x; partly-known, a patent family and forum request exist); provisional streaming from a 64-token block (speed idx0, about 1.0x because block 1 already touches about 72% of experts and the tokens come from a truncated prompt).
arithmetic_errors_found: Prefill baseline: the 109 s cold TTFT uses the 55 GFLOP/s decode GEMV rate for prefill. Measured batched prefill is 311 GFLOP/s (5.7x higher), so compute is 6e12/311e9 = 19.3 s. Prefill is I/O-bound at 22-44 s (69 GB at 3.1, 2.4 or 1.56 GB/s). Hit in idx0, idx3, idx13, speed0, r7-2, and r7-3 (idx3 there is the dispatch idea).
Prefill I/O ignored: a 64-token block already touches about 72% of experts (about 49 GB) and 500 tokens touch nearly all 69 GB (speed0, r7-2, idx13).

Read-rate mixing: the 4 MiB rate (2.4 GB/s) is applied to tensors of about 0.9 MB (1.56 GB/s at 1 MiB reads) in idx0. idx5 and speed5 mix the 2.4 and 3.1 GB/s rates, which double-counts the read-size gain already in the baseline.

Wrong baseline (uncached, serial, or plain mmap instead of our best path of 2.18 serial / 4.16 overlap at 8 GB, about 4.19 and 4.27 at 16 and 32 GB): idx1, idx4, idx5, idx8, idx11, idx12, idx14, idx15, idx18, idx9, speed5, idx2, r7-1, idx7. Examples: idx11 uses 1.2 tok/s, idx5 uses 1.85 tok/s, idx1 uses a serial 1.8 tok/s.

Compute ceiling of 4.57 tok/s exceeded or ignored: idx5 claims 6.6 tok/s, idx9 claims 5-9, idx15 and idx18 claim up to 8, idx2 claims 37, idx8 and idx16 scale the ceiling with bits or k. 2-bit does not cut FLOPs.
Dense share ignored (idx16): only about 40% of the 12 GFLOP is experts (4.9 expert, 7.1 dense). Top-4 gives a 6.0 tok/s ceiling (1.31x), not 11.5.

Double counting of cache or bytes: idx4 counts the 0.72 GB prefetch as hidden and also subtracts it from the 1.3 GB (wrong prefetches use the same disk, so 1.3 GB are still read). idx12 multiplies a 42% reuse into the no-cache 1.3 GB base. idx19 counts k=8 grouping the LRU already absorbs. idx7 counts hit rate from cache size as a pinning gain. idx14 attributes to ARC and a network tier what plain LRU at 3 footprints already gives (0.4 GB/token).
Window error (idx4): the lead time is one layer (about 4.6 ms against 8.7 ms to read 27 MB), not a token. The 0.55 precision is in-sample; held out it is 0.31-0.43.

Straggler ignored (idx10): the busier node does 1.25-1.28x its fair share on the real traces, so the two-node compute ceiling is about 7.3 tok/s, not 9.2. 48 round trips add about 15 ms, and no cache credit is taken.

Internal inconsistencies: idx9 headline 1.3/0.54 = 2.4x is below its own '3x' and a 2-bit base of 69 GB is about 32 GB, not 24. idx19 says residual 1.9x but quotes 331 MB (3.93x); 1.3 GB/1.9 = 684 MB. idx5 says 2-3 bit residuals give 3.6x fewer bytes but 2.5/4.3 gives at most 1.7x. idx2 says about 3x fewer bytes but 4.3/2.4 = 1.79x. idx8 says 1.3 bpw but an 8-bit index per 8 weights is 1.0 bpw. idx15 says 2.7 tok/s but 1/(0.26+0.22) = 2.1. idx12 says 6.3 tok/s from 0.38 GB, but I/O alone allows 8.2 tok/s and compute allows 4.57. idx11 says 38 layers fit in 16 GB, but that is about 53 GB.

Capacity and hardware: idx7 assumes a 20 GB pin on an 8 GB machine (1.9 GB dense leaves 4-5 GB, about 2 footprints). Peer ideas assume 25GbE, RDMA or 100GbE and a 69 GB peer; practical rates are 0.12-1.15 GB/s on 1-10 GbE.

Metric confusion: TTFT ratios (109 s to 14 s, 3.7x, 40x) are presented as speed-ups, and idx3 and r7-2 call them 'perceived 3-4x tok/s'. Decode tok/s is unchanged. idx3 also overstates KV size at 1-2 GB for 500 tokens; GQA gives about 50-150 MB.

Dispatch count (r7-3): 23k launches comes from 480 slices x 48 layers, but ggml issues about 144 graph ops per token. Measured rates already include dispatch, so removing a '60% overhead' double-counts.

Zero-cost assumption (r7-4, jump-forward): forced tokens still need a batched forward and touch more unique experts (19.6 per layer for 4 tokens). The ceiling at f=0.7 is about 2.7x, not 3.3x. r7-1 ignores verify-pass expert I/O.
Chunked typing-time prefill (idx13, r7-2): re-reads about 8x the expert bytes of one batched prefill, and per-chunk time (about 9 s) exceeds typing fill time (3-5 s per 25 tokens).

Low-rank (idx17): rank 64 keeps only about 3-4% of the ranks of 1.5-2k-rank expert matrices. A basis plus rank-r residual is a rank-2r truncation, not lossless. The 55 GFLOP/s rate is assumed for skinny rank-64 GEMVs, which will not reach it. idx1 combines the CPU's 55 GFLOP/s with unproven FPGA compute.
ranked.honest_headline: No candidate qualifies as revolutionary. Only layer skipping reaches 3x or more over our best path (about 3.0-3.2x at 16 and 32 GB at 67% of layers skipped), and it is published (Dr.LLM, ShortGPT, LayerSkip) and has no quality support. Its realistic range is 1.1-1.4x. Everything else is 1.0-2.1x against our best path and is known or partly known. Compute-ceiling lifters, the only ones that matter at 16 and 32 GB where the 4.57 tok/s decode ceiling binds: layer skipping (rank 1), multi-node expert parallelism (2, needs a second machine), top-k reduction (3, about 6.0 tok/s ceiling), shared-basis low-rank (4, possible compute lifter only in the optimistic variant), intra-expert sparsity (5), the LUT kernel half of VQ (6, unproven), and batched-verify speculation (7 and 8, partial lifters limited by expert I/O). The I/O-only ideas cap at about 1.0-1.1x at 16 and 32 GB. The nearest near-miss on novelty is typing-time prefill (partly-known). It is TTFT-only, so it fails the criteria.
